descripcion_es: Possession, family, appearance and illnesses; questions and negatives.
resumen: Have and have got mean “to possess” (es: tener): possessions, family, physical features, illnesses. Have works like a normal verb with do/does; have got uses have/has as an auxiliary and is more common in spoken British English.

explicacion.texto: To talk about possession both forms are correct: I have a car = I've got a car. The important thing is not to mix their structures in questions and negatives.

filas: Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't.

items: In the third person singular: has / has got (he's got).
Have got is only used in the present; in the past we say had (I had a bike).
Have (not have got) is also used in action expressions: have breakfast, have a shower, have a good time.
Hunger, thirst and age are not expressed with have, but with to be.

ejemplos.frase: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
My grandmother has got blue eyes.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi abuela tiene los ojos azules.

ejemplos.frase: He doesn't have a mobile phone.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: In modern English a question with have needs do (or else Have you got a car?).

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: She don't have got a dog.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Don't mix do with have got.
In the third person singular: has.

ejercicios.explicacion: The agreement rule for have applies: has only in the third person singular and have for the rest. The clue is the subject My neighbours, plural, which is equivalent to they. So the form is have. A subject ending in -s doesn't mean the verb takes -s: it is exactly the opposite.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: My neighbours is equivalent to they: have.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mis vecinos tienen un jardín precioso.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Has is only for he, she, it or a singular noun; my neighbours is plural.
Have meaning possession is a state verb and is not used in the continuous form.
Have doesn't take -s in the plural; the third person singular form is has.

ejercicios.explicacion: The third person singular rule applies: with he, she, it or a singular proper name, have becomes has. The clue is the subject Ana, which is equivalent to she. The unit also reminds you that have is used for physical features, such as hair. Note that in English hair is uncountable here and takes no article: long black hair.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ana tiene el pelo largo y negro.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It is the typical mistake in the unit (He have…): with a third person singular subject we use has.
It is a calque of Spanish structures such as “es de pelo largo”; for physical features we use has.
The third person of have is irregular: has.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the negative form of have got.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for the negative of have got applies: the negative goes directly with have, without do: haven't got. The clue is the subject I and the instruction to use the negative form. Any is the usual form in negatives with uncountable nouns (money). Both the contracted form haven't got, the most common in speech, and the full form have not got, more emphatic or written, are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Negative of have got: haven't got.
ejercicios.traduccion: No llevo nada de dinero encima.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes the two structures: with have got the negative is haven't got, without do.
With I we use have, not has.
Got is missing: without it, the negative with have needs do (I don't have).

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the unit applies: have as a normal verb forms questions with do/does. The clue is the subject your flat, which is equivalent to it (third person singular), and the verb have in the base form after it. So the auxiliary is Does. Does carries the third-person -s, and have stays unchanged.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Your flat is equivalent to it: does + have.

errores_previstos.explicacion: With a third person singular subject (your flat = it) we use does.
Has your flat…? would need got (Has your flat got a balcony?); with have in the base form after it, we use does.
Be doesn't form questions with have; the auxiliary is does.

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for questions with have got applies: have swaps places with the subject and got stays after it. The clue is got after you: it shows that the structure is have got. So the question starts with Have. The unit insists on not mixing the two structures.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With have got the question starts with have.

por_opcion.Do: Incorrect: do is used with have as a normal verb (Do you have a pen?), not with have got.
por_opcion.Have: Correct: with have got the question is formed by swapping have and the subject.
por_opcion.Are: Incorrect: be has nothing to do with have got; “Are you got” doesn't exist.

ejercicios.explicacion: The agreement rule for have got applies: with he, she and it we use has got. The clue is the subject He. The unit also reminds you that have is used for illnesses: a cold. In Spanish we say “está resfriado”, but in English you “have” a cold.

por_opcion.has got: Correct: third person singular, has got.
por_opcion.have got: Incorrect: have got is for I, you, we and they; with he we use has got.
por_opcion.is: Incorrect: it is a calque of Spanish “está resfriado”; he is a cold would mean that he himself is a cold.

ejercicios.frase: Do you have a dog? No, I ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the unit on short answers applies: if the question uses do, so does the short answer. The clue is Do you have…?, a question with have as a normal verb. With I the answer is No, I don't. Don't mix it with the have got structure.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If the question uses do, so does the short answer.

por_opcion.haven't: Incorrect according to the rule in the unit: it answers with the have got structure to a question made with do. In British English you sometimes hear No, I haven't, but the consistent answer is I don't.
por_opcion.don't: Correct: the short answer repeats the auxiliary of the question, do.
por_opcion.doesn't: Incorrect: doesn't is for the third person singular; with I we use don't.

ejercicios.frase: Has she got a bike? Yes, she ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for short answers applies: repeat the auxiliary of the question. The clue is Has she got…?, a question with have got, so the answer uses has: Yes, she has. In the short answer you don't add got.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Question with has got: answer with has.

por_opcion.has: Correct: the question uses has got and the short answer repeats has.
por_opcion.does: Incorrect: does answers questions with does have, not with has got.
por_opcion.is: Incorrect: be doesn't answer questions with have.

ejercicios.enunciado: Turn the sentence into a question with have got.
ejercicios.frase: They have got a new car.
respuestas: Have they got a new car?
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for questions with have got applies: swap have and the subject, and got stays after the subject. The clue is the instruction to form a question with have got from They have got. The result is Have they got a new car?, without do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do they have got a new car?
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes the two structures: have got doesn't use do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Have got they a new car?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Got goes after the subject: Have they got…?

errores_previstos.respuesta: They have got a new car?
errores_previstos.explicacion: It only adds a question mark; you need to swap have and the subject.

ejercicios.enunciado: Make the sentence negative using do/does.
respuestas: She does not have a laptop.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for have as a normal verb applies: the negative is formed with doesn't + have. The clue is the instruction to use do/does and the subject she, third person singular. The -s moves to does and have stays in the base form: She doesn't have a laptop. Does not is also accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With have as a normal verb: doesn't + have.

errores_previstos.explicacion: After doesn't the verb is in the base form: have.
With she we use doesn't, not don't.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She doesn't have got a laptop.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes the two structures, as in the typical mistake in the unit: either doesn't have or hasn't got.

ejercicios.frase: My brother have got three children.
respuestas: My brother has got three children.
ejercicios.explicacion: The agreement rule applies: with a third person singular subject we use has got. The clue is My brother, which is equivalent to he. You need to change have got to has got; the contraction My brother's got is also accepted.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My brother have got three children.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: with my brother we use has got.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My brother has get three children.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The form is has got, not has get.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My brother haves got three children.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The third person of have is irregular: has.

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the unit applies: after does the verb is in the base form. The clue is Does at the beginning: does already carries the third-person marker, so has must go back to have. It is a very common mistake because learners think of “he has” and keep it.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After does comes the base form have.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: after does comes the base form have.
With he the auxiliary is does, not do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Does he have got a passport?
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes does with have got; we say Does he have…? or Has he got…?

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the unit applies: age is expressed with to be, not with have. The clue is the structure “tengo X años”, which Spanish speakers calque word for word. The correct form is I am 25 years old or simply I am 25 (or I'm 25). What you can't say is “I am 25 years” without old.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Age is expressed with to be.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: age is expressed with be.
Changing to have got doesn't fix the calque; age goes with be.
With years you need old: I am 25 years old (or just I am 25).

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the words in order to make a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for questions with have got applies: have + subject + got + object. The clue is the instruction to form a question and the presence of have and got together. Any is used in questions with plurals: any pets. The final order is Have you got any pets.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Got goes after the subject: Have you got…
That is the affirmative word order; in the question have goes before the subject.

descripcion_larga_es: Have and have got mean “to possess” (es: tener) and are used to talk about possessions, family, physical appearance and illnesses. Have works like a normal verb and forms questions and negatives with do/does; have got uses have/has as an auxiliary and is very common in spoken British English. The difficult part for Spanish speakers is not mixing the two structures and not using have for age.

contexto.que_es: They are two ways of expressing possession or belonging with the same meaning (es: tener). Have is a main verb that needs do/does in questions and negatives and becomes has in the third person. Have got is a compound form in which have/has acts as an auxiliary: it is inverted in questions and made negative directly (haven't got).
contexto.por_que_importa: Talking about what you have (family, home, objects, symptoms) is one of the first things you do in another language. Mixing the two structures (Does he has…?, She don't have got…) is a very noticeable mistake even at high levels. Also, knowing have got is necessary to understand spoken British English, where it is more common than have.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It is used for possessions (a car), relationships (two brothers), physical features (long hair), illnesses (a cold) and features of things (a balcony). Short answers repeat the auxiliary of the question: Do you…? No, I don't; Have you got…? Yes, I have. Spanish speakers often calque “tengo 25 años” with have, when in English age is expressed with be.
